newsitem.title: USA: Stocks criminal attended coffee with Clinton - Post.
newsitem.headline: Stocks criminal attended coffee with Clinton - Post.

text.p: A New Jersey stock promoter convicted of criminal securities fraud was among eight guests who accepted an invitation to join President Clinton and top Democratic party leaders for coffee at the White House in 1995, the Washington Post reported Saturday.

Eric Wynn, whose stock manipulation benefited a member of the Bonanno organised crime family, bilked millions from investors and served two years in prison after a 1989 guilty plea on theft and tax charges, the newspaper said.

An unidentified close associate of Wynn's quoted in the report said Wynn was trying to obtain a pardon for his July 21, 1995, stock manipulation conviction. A Justice Department spokesman told the Post there was no record of any formal request by Wynn for a pardon.

The newspaper said it was unclear who had issued the White House invitation to Wynn. It added that he was brought into Democratic fund-raising circles by Richard Mays, an Arkansas lawyer who served as a Clinton appointee on the Arkansas Supreme Court in the early 1980s.

Wynn's second conviction occurred five months before the Dec. 21, 1995, coffee meeting with Clinton. He was sentenced in September to 52 months in prison and ordered to pay a $50,000 fine. Wynn is free on bail while appealing the conviction, the Post said.

The White House has been embarrassed by disclosures that guests at functions over the past four years have included a convicted drug dealer and the owner of a Chinese arms company now under investigation by U.S. authorities.
Questions have arisen about Clinton's White House coffee chats with wealthy people, many of whom later contributed large sums to the Democrats -- a reported total of $27 million.

Clinton has insisted no laws were broken in the way Democrats attracted donors. But there have been so many questions raised that Republicans in Congress are promising oversight hearings and want Clinton to appoint an independent counsel to investigate.

A 25-agent FBI task force has been assigned to probe the activities of former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang, who tapped Asian-American sources for about $2.5 million. About $1.5 million was returned because of questions as to whether it came from foreign sources, which would be illegal.
Clinton defended the White House coffee sessions in general, but acknowledged that mistakes had been made in fund-raising.

At a news conference Tuesday he said it had been inappropriate for a U.S. government regulator to attend a coffee at the White House organised by the Democratic National Committee for the leaders of 17 major financial institutions.

The regulator, Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig, who said he was unaware the session had been set up by the DNC and that he would not have attended had he known, wields considerable power over those potential donors.
